name: Pantheon
info: The Pantheon is a Roman temple in Rome, first built by Marcus Agrippa under Augustus and rebuilt under Hadrian, probably dedicated about 126; a church since 609, its dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

facts.made: First built by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa in the reign of Augustus; the present building completed by Hadrian, with Lise Hetland dating its start to 114 under Trajan and some scholars naming Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus
facts.form: A round brick-faced concrete rotunda under a coffered dome with an open oculus, the interior 43.3 metres high and wide, fronted by a portico of granite Corinthian columns under a pediment and linked to it by a rectangular block
facts.where: Piazza della Rotonda in the centre of Rome; a state property, still in use as the Basilica of Saint Mary and the Martyrs
facts.known: the largest unreinforced concrete dome; the oculus and its moving circle of light; Agrippa's inscription on Hadrian's building; conversion to a church in 609; the tombs of Raphael and Italy's kings; its copies across Western architecture

t: The present building replaced Agrippa's temple after fires in 80 and 110, yet carries Agrippa's inscription, so its date and even its original purpose remain uncertain.
Its consecration as a church in 609 saved it from the abandonment and worst spoliation that befell most of ancient Rome's buildings.
As the best-preserved Roman monumental building, it has served as a model for domes and porticoes from Brunelleschi's Florence to Jefferson's University of Virginia.
dyk: The oculus has never been covered, so rain falls on the floor, which slopes about 30 centimetres to its drains; at Pentecost firefighters throw red rose petals through it from the roof.
ev: Marcus Agrippa built the first Pantheon as part of a complex on his own property in the Campus Martius
The Augustan Pantheon was destroyed by fire; Domitian rebuilt it, and it burned again in 110
The present building, completed by Hadrian, was probably dedicated
Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored the building, damaged by age, and recorded it on the architrave
The Byzantine emperor Phocas gave the building to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it to St. Mary and the Martyrs
The emperor Constans II stripped the bronze roof tiles and sent them to Constantinople
Pope Urban VIII had the bronze trusses of the portico melted down, most of it for cannon
Extensive restoration of the dome, brickwork and floor began during the Fascist period

sections.origins:
After the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa began a building programme on his own property in the Campus Martius, creating in 29–19 BCE a complex of three buildings aligned from south to north: the Baths of Agrippa, the Basilica of Neptune and the Pantheon. The Pantheon and the basilica seem to have been Agrippa's private sacred buildings rather than public temples, which may explain how the building could lose its original name and purpose; Adam Ziolkowski contends it was first the Temple of Mars in Campo. Pliny the Elder, the only eyewitness to describe it, records capitals of Syracusan bronze, caryatids by Diogenes of Athens and one of Cleopatra's pearls cut in half as earrings for a statue of Venus.

The form of Agrippa's building is debated. Rodolfo Lanciani concluded from late 19th-century excavations that it faced south with a shortened T-shaped plan; later diggers proposed a round building with a porch facing north, a view Ziolkowski rejects as surmise. The name, from the Greek Pantheion, 'of all the gods', is itself uncertain: Cassius Dio thought it came from the statues of many gods or from the dome's likeness to the heavens, and Ziolkowski takes it to have been a nickname rather than a formal name.
sections.content:
The building is round in plan except for its portico of large granite Corinthian columns, eight in the front rank and two groups of four behind, under a pediment once decorated with relief sculpture, probably of gilded bronze and probably an eagle within a wreath. A rectangular block links the porch to the rotunda, whose bronze doors, 7.53 metres high, are the oldest in Rome and have been shown to be the original Roman doors. Two niches at the back of the portico were perhaps meant for statues of Augustus and Agrippa.

Inside, the height to the oculus equals the diameter of the circle, 43.3 metres, so a sphere would fit within the interior. The dome spans 150 Roman feet and its oculus 30. The oculus and the door are the only sources of natural light, and the light from the oculus moves around the room through the day, marking time with light rather than shadow. The dome has five rings of 28 sunken coffers, which in antiquity may have held bronze rosettes; its interior was possibly meant to stand for the vault of the heavens. Circles and squares unify the design, though each zone from floor to ceiling follows its own scheme. How the building was used in antiquity is not known.
sections.making:
The Augustan Pantheon burned in 80 CE; Domitian rebuilt it, and it burned again in 110. The present building was completed by Hadrian and probably dedicated about 126, but its date is uncertain, because Hadrian re-inscribed it with Agrippa's original text: 'Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, made this when consul for the third time.' Lise Hetland argues that construction began in 114 under Trajan, challenging Herbert Bloch's 1959 brick-stamp study behind the usual Hadrianic date, and Heilmeyer names Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus on stylistic grounds.

The 4,535-tonne dome thins from 6.4 metres at its base to 1.2 metres at the oculus, and its aggregate grows lighter as it rises, from travertine to terracotta tiles to tufa and pumice; Mark and Hutchison estimated that ordinary concrete throughout would have raised the stresses by some 80 percent. Relieving arches, hidden chambers and eight barrel vaults carry the load into eight piers. The portico's grey granite columns came from Mons Claudianus in Egypt and its pink ones from Aswan, each 11.9 metres tall and 60 tonnes, dragged to the Nile, shipped to Ostia and pulled up the Tiber. Remains of a higher second pediment suggest that taller 50-foot columns were planned, and scholars debate why shorter ones were used.
sections.reception:
Writing about 75 years after the rebuilding, Cassius Dio wrongly credited the domed building to Agrippa; even by 200 its origin and purpose were uncertain. Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored it in 202, 'damaged by age, with all its adornments', and added their own inscription. In 609 the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave it to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it on 13 May 609 as a church of St. Mary and the Martyrs; twenty-eight cartloads of martyrs' relics were said to have been brought from the catacombs and placed beneath the high altar, with an icon of the Virgin.

From the Renaissance it became a place of burial and of artistic devotion. The painters Raphael and Annibale Carracci, the composer Arcangelo Corelli and the architect Baldassare Peruzzi are buried there, and a 16th-century confraternity of artists and musicians, later joined by Bernini, Cortona and Algardi, kept up worship in one chapel; it survives as the Pontifical Academy of Fine Arts. Filippo Brunelleschi was among the architects who looked to the building for inspiration. After Italian unification, Vittorio Emanuele II, Umberto I and Queen Margherita were buried there, and an honour guard still stands at the royal tombs.
sections.survival:
Its continuous use explains why the Pantheon is among the best preserved of all Roman buildings. Even so, Constans II stripped its bronze roof tiles in 663, and the rotunda stayed uncovered for nearly a century until Pope Gregory III lined it with lead. Exterior marble and the pediment's sculptures were lost, three eastern columns fell and were buttressed by a wall, and vendor stalls crowded the portico. After the Avignon Papacy, Martin V and Nicholas V renewed the roof and Eugene IV cleared the portico and paved the piazza. Many relics were looted or destroyed in the Sack of Rome in 1527.

Urban VIII melted down the bronze trusses of the portico, mostly for cannon, prompting the satirists' line 'What the barbarians did not do the Barberinis did'; he and Alexander VII also restored the missing columns. Twin bell towers by Maderno and Borromini, nicknamed 'the ass's ears', stood until 1883. In 1753 Paolo Posi remodelled the attic in Neoclassical taste, a change heavily criticised and partly reversed in the 1930s. Restoration from 1928 renewed the dome's plaster, brickwork and floor, the doors were repaired in 1998, and work in 2004–2005 dealt with water damage.
sections.legacy:
The Pantheon's combination of a large circular domed cella with a conventional temple portico was unique in Roman architecture, yet it became a standard model whenever classical styles were revived. Its influence runs from Brunelleschi's dome of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence, completed in 1436, through Bernini's Santa Maria Assunta in Ariccia (1664), St. Hedwig's Cathedral in Berlin, Belle Isle House in England and the Rotunda of Mosta in Malta. Thomas Jefferson relied on Palladio's engravings of it for the Rotunda of the University of Virginia, and its portico-and-dome form appears in many city halls, universities and libraries of the 19th and 20th centuries; Albert Speer's unbuilt Volkshalle also drew on it.

Since the French Revolution, when the church of Sainte-Geneviève became the Panthéon of Paris, the word has also named buildings that honour the illustrious dead. The Roman building remains a working Catholic church, with Mass on Sundays and holy days and occasional weddings, and is managed by Italy's Ministry of Culture. Since 2025 visitors can also pass into the adjoining Basilica of Neptune.

summary: The Pantheon in Rome was founded by Marcus Agrippa and rebuilt under Hadrian, probably dedicated about 126, with an unreinforced concrete dome that is still the largest of its kind. Made a church in 609, it survived better than almost any other Roman building and became a model for domed buildings across the Western world.
